tasks.title: Read the hardware of two instance types and your metadata defaults
tasks.kills: "A Graviton instance can run the same AMI as an x86 instance."
tasks.plan: In AWS CloudShell, read-only, 3 minutes, $0. (1) aws ec2 describe-instance-types --instance-types t3.micro r7g.large with a --query that prints InstanceType, VCpuInfo.DefaultVCpus, MemoryInfo.SizeInMiB, ProcessorInfo.SupportedArchitectures, BurstablePerformanceSupported and HibernationSupported, --output table: the expected output shows an x86_64 burstable type and an arm64 memory optimized type, so an AMI built for one architecture does not fit the other (ec2-resize-same-processor-architecture, ec2-instance-type-name-structure). (2) aws ec2 describe-instance-types --filters Name=hibernation-supported,Values=false with a short --query on InstanceType and --max-items 10: the expected output lists types that cannot hibernate (ec2-hibernate-supported-families-no-bare-metal). (3) aws ec2 get-instance-metadata-defaults: the expected output shows the account's metadata defaults for the Region, which may be empty (ec2-imds-account-default-v2-new-instances). Creates nothing. The writer confirms the filter name, the query fields and get-instance-metadata-defaults with tasks check-cli --reference; drop step 3 if the reference does not list it.

tasks.title: Launch from a launch template then watch the public address change
tasks.kills: "A stopped and started instance keeps its public IPv4 address."
tasks.plan: In AWS CloudShell, in the default VPC, about 20 minutes. Cost line: one small instance billed per second while running with a [60-second minimum] (ec2-on-demand-billing-per-second-60s-minimum), plus public IPv4 address charges for the auto-assigned address and the Elastic IP address (ec2-eip-charged-in-use-and-idle); state an amount only from a verified pricing fact, else name the dimensions as chapter 14 did. No key pair, no SSH. Steps: capture the default VPC ID; create security group saa-ec2-t02 with no inbound rule, tagged book=saa and task=ec2-t02; create launch template saa-ec2-t02 (tag the template itself book=saa, task=ec2-t02) with ImageId resolve:ssm:/aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-x86_64 (Amazon Linux 2023, not Amazon Linux 2), InstanceType t3.micro, the security group, MetadataOptions HttpTokens=required, and instance TagSpecifications book=saa and task=ec2-t02 (ec2-launch-template-stores-launch-parameters); run-instances --launch-template LaunchTemplateName=saa-ec2-t02 (capture INSTANCE_ID); aws ec2 wait instance-running; describe-instances and read PublicIpAddress and PrivateIpAddress. Break it: predict 'Will the public IPv4 address stay the same after a stop and start?'; stop-instances, wait instance-stopped, start-instances, wait instance-running, describe again: expect a different public address and the same private address; explain [The instance gets a new public IPv4 address] (ec2-state-diff-public-ipv4) and it [keeps its private IPv4 address] (ec2-state-diff-private-ipv4). Fix: allocate-address (tagged book=saa, task=ec2-t02; capture ALLOC_ID) and associate-address with the instance; stop and start again; the address stays: it [remains associated with the instance] (ec2-state-diff-elastic-ip). Cleanup in reverse order: disassociate-address, release-address, terminate-instances, wait instance-terminated, delete-launch-template, delete-security-group. Verify: aws resourcegroupstaggingapi get-resources --tag-filters Key=task,Values=ec2-t02, expect nothing after cleanup; if a terminated instance can still be listed for a short while (ec2-terminated-instance-cannot-recover: 'visible in the console for a short while'), use the T108 by-name verify instead: aws ec2 describe-launch-templates --launch-template-names saa-ec2-t02, expect a not-found error. Label 'checked against docs, not run in a real account'. The writer confirms the resolve:ssm form for a launch template ImageId with tasks check-cli --reference.

tasks.title: Hibernate an instance and see why another one cannot
tasks.kills: "You can hibernate any running instance whenever you want to keep its memory."
tasks.plan: In AWS CloudShell, in the default VPC, about 25 minutes. Cost line: two small instances billed per second while running, EBS storage while hibernated with no instance usage fee (ec2-hibernate-no-instance-fee-ebs-rates), and public IPv4 address charges (ec2-eip-charged-in-use-and-idle); amounts only from verified pricing facts. No key pair, no SSH. Steps: create security group saa-ec2-t03 with no inbound rule (tags book=saa, task=ec2-t03). Launch instance A from the Amazon Linux 2023 SSM parameter, type t3.micro, with --hibernation-options Configured=true and a block device mapping that sets the root volume Encrypted=true (ec2-hibernate-enable-only-at-launch, ec2-hibernate-root-volume-requirements), tagged book=saa and task=ec2-t03 (capture A_ID); launch instance B the same way without hibernation options (capture B_ID); wait instance-status-ok for both. stop-instances --instance-ids $A_ID --hibernate; wait instance-stopped; describe-instances and read StateReason.Code: expect Client.UserInitiatedHibernate (ec2-faq-hibernate-state-reason) and state stopped (ec2-faq-hibernated-state-is-stopped). Break it: predict 'Can you hibernate instance B now?'; stop-instances --instance-ids $B_ID --hibernate: expect an error; explain that you [can't enable hibernation on an existing instance] (ec2-hibernate-enable-only-at-launch). Fix: no command turns it on for B; stop B normally (its RAM is cleared, ec2-faq-hibernate-vs-stop-ram) and, for a real workload, launch a replacement with hibernation configured. Start A: [the RAM contents are reloaded] (ec2-hibernate-saves-ram-to-root-volume). Cleanup: terminate-instances for A and B, wait instance-terminated, delete-security-group. speak.prompt: The instance is at 9% most of the day. Are we paying for a size that we do not need?
speak.note: Ana uses no AWS terms: explain 'instance' as 'the rented server' the first time and 'burstable' as 'a size that saves unused power for busy hours'. Short answer: probably yes; at 9% most of the day the server is bigger than it needs to be, and a smaller size that can burst costs less. How it works: AWS tools compare the size with the measured use; a burstable size saves the quiet hours as credits and spends them in the morning peak. Watch: changing the size needs a short stop, and the 85% morning peak must still fit. In your case: 'Can we take a short maintenance window on a weekday night?' Must not say: 'AWS resizes the server while it runs'; 'a smaller server is free at night'; 'the morning peak no longer matters'.

speak.persona: a startup founder in office hours
speak.prompt: Should we buy a Savings Plan, or just run everything on Spot to save money?
speak.note: First sentence starts 'Both': both lower the price, but for different work. Short answer: a Savings Plan for the steady base that runs all year, Spot for work that can stop and restart, On-Demand for the rest. How it works: the Savings Plan is a commitment to spend per hour for one or three years; Spot uses spare capacity that AWS can take back with two minutes of warning. Watch: never put the database or a job with a hard deadline on Spot; and a Savings Plan is a discount, not reserved capacity. In your case: 'Which of your jobs can restart if a server disappears?' Must not say: 'a high maximum price keeps Spot from being interrupted'; 'a Savings Plan guarantees capacity'; 'Spot is fine for the database'.

speak.prompt: Our engineers SSH into production servers from home. How do we close port 22 and still fix things?
speak.note: Short answer: use Session Manager: engineers get a shell with no open port, no SSH keys and no bastion host. How it works: each server gets a role with one AWS managed policy for Systems Manager, and the security group keeps no inbound rule for SSH. Watch: a server without that role does not show up for Session Manager; and do not describe how the agent reaches Systems Manager until fr-0061 is filled. In your case: 'Does anyone need a real SSH client, for example to copy files? Then look at EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint.' Must not say: 'restrict port 22 to the office IP address and you are done'; 'you need a bastion host in a public subnet'; 'store an access key on the server for the agent'.

speak.persona: an ML startup CTO you advise
speak.prompt: Our service loads a large model into memory for 20 minutes every morning. Can we switch the servers off at night without that wait?
speak.note: Short answer: yes, hibernate them; the memory is written to the disk at night and loaded back in the morning. How it works: hibernation saves memory to the encrypted root volume; at night you pay for the disk, not for the server. Watch: it works only if hibernation was turned on when the servers were launched, the memory fits the limit of one hundred fifty gibibytes on Linux, and the servers are not in an Auto Scaling group. In your case: 'How much memory does each server have, and do they run in an Auto Scaling group?' Must not say: 'you can turn hibernation on for the running servers tonight'; 'you pay nothing while they hibernate'; 'any instance size can hibernate'. Numbers as words, from the fact cards.

diagrams.claim: An instance starts from an AMI and an instance type, runs in one Availability Zone, and is billed while it runs.

Amazon EC2 places the instance in a subnet, which sits in one Availability Zone.
The AMI provides the software that sets up and boots the instance.
The instance type determines the hardware that the instance gets.
Code on the instance gets temporary credentials of its role from the instance metadata service.
Billing runs for the seconds the instance is in the running state.

diagrams.title: The states of an instance
diagrams.claim: A stopped instance can start again, but a terminated instance is gone for good.
diagrams.alt: A state diagram with six states: pending, running, stopping, stopped, shutting-down and terminated. Launch leads to pending and running; stop leads through stopping to stopped; start leads back to pending; terminate leads through shutting-down to terminated, which is final.

diagrams.claim: A cluster group packs instances close together, while spread and partition groups keep them on separate hardware.
diagrams.alt: Three panels. Cluster: four instances on racks next to each other in one zone. Spread: each instance on its own rack, across two zones. Partition: two partitions, each a group of racks with several instances, across two zones.

diagrams.title: How do you pay for an instance?
diagrams.claim: Licensing, tolerance for interruption and steady use decide how you pay for an instance.
diagrams.alt: A decision ladder with three questions. Licenses bound to sockets or cores lead to Dedicated Hosts; work that can stop and restart leads to Spot Instances; steady use for one or three years leads to a Savings Plan; everything else leads to On-Demand.
